title: Boise Fire to conduct live training all day Tuesday
summary: Boise Fire is conducting a live-fire training exercise at 2605 S. Utter Street, just west of the Timberline High School track, between 8 a.m. and 7 p.m. on November 24.
text:
BOISE, Idaho — Heads up to Boise residents on Tuesday.
Boise Fire is conducting a live-fire training exercise at 2605 S. Utter Street, just west of the Timberline High School track, between 8 a.m. and 7 p.m. on November 24.
Neighbors and drivers passing through the area may see smoke during the exercise.
Safety officers will be on site supervising the scene.
People are being asked to stay clear of the area for safety reasons.

title: Federal official highlights Idaho’s success in increasing foster home-to-child ratio
summary: Idaho’s former state health director, now a federal official in the Trump administration, is highlighting Idaho’s success in increasing the ratio of foster families to foster children to kindle “healthy competition” among state child welfare programs. Federal Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams traveled to Boise on Monday to meet with state, […]
text:
Federal official highlights Idaho’s success in increasing foster home-to-child ratio
Idaho ranks first in the nation for this ratio. Some counties still lack enough foster homes.
Assistant Secretary at the Administration for Children and Families Alex Adams speaks to a group of state, local and nonprofit officials about Idaho’s success in improving the ratio of foster children to foster families on Nov. 23, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Laura Guido / Idaho Capital Sun)
Idaho’s former state health director, now a federal official in the Trump administration, is highlighting Idaho’s success in increasing the ratio of foster families to foster children to kindle “healthy competition” among state child welfare programs.
Federal Administration for Children and Families Assistant Secretary Alex Adams traveled to Boise on Monday to meet with state, local and nonprofit officials to discuss the Gem State’s changes to the foster care system and announce a federal competition among the states.
“We put out the first incarnation of the scorecard showing each state’s performance on those measures, and perhaps not surprisingly, Idaho is currently in the pole position,” Adams said Monday.
The federal administration’s recently launched child welfare “scorecard” shows certain metrics: foster-home-to-foster-children ratios, family placement (known as kin placement, in which the foster child is placed with a relative) rates, use of congregate care facilities, recent maltreatment case percentages, and disrupted home placement rates.
As of Monday, Idaho ranked first in its ratio of foster homes per foster child, at 116 homes for every 100 foster children in the system. Data for 27 states was available Monday, and all 50 states would be added by the end of December, Adams said.
From Oct. 1, 2027, to Sept. 30, 2027, the Administration for Children and Families will host a challenge for state child welfare systems, in which the state with the highest foster-home-to-foster-child ratio will win $3 million from the federal agency, followed by $2 million for the second-highest, and $1 million each for the two states with the most improved ratios.
“When we announced this competition, it was really that we wanted healthy competition across state lines for the betterment of child welfare outcomes,” Adams said.
    Idaho’s foster ratio increased substantially statewide. Some regions still lack enough foster homes. 
Before Adams was tapped for his federal post within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, he served as director of Idaho’s state Department of Health and Welfare for just over a year.
At the time, he highlighted a major focus on ensuring that there was at least one foster home available for every foster child entering the system. The Legislature in 2025 approved an additional $23 million to the state agency for child welfare changes, including an increased focus on prevention and recruitment and retention of foster parents.

title: From Kabul to Boise: Afghan women rebuild their dreams in Idaho
summary: Two young Afghan women rebuilding their lives in Idaho share their fight to get education.
text:
Since the fall of Kabul in 2021, more than 1,000 Afghan evacuees have resettled in Idaho – most of them right here in the Boise area. Two young Afghan women who are rebuilding their lives and pursuing their dreams in Idaho reflect back on their journey to education.
Five years ago, Ramzia Jalali was sitting inside a lecture hall at Kabul University, dreaming of her future. Within hours, the Taliban entered the city, and her world froze.
"When I was in Afghanistan, I was a medical student. I was in my third semester at Kabul University, and I had many dreams for my life, for my future," Jalali said. "I wanted to become a successful doctor, and I wanted to help the people. When the Taliban entered Kabul on August 15, 2021, everything changed."
Thousands of people tried to flee as the country fell into chaos. Videos published by NPR showed desperate crowds rushing to the Kabul airport amid gunfire.
"I felt at that time I lost my hopes, my dreams, my life, my education and everything," Jalali said.
Starting over in the American West
Jalali is not alone. What was once an unfamiliar city in the American West has become a refuge for young Afghan women whose desire to learn was abruptly cut short back home. Still, starting life over in Boise came with steep challenges.
"It's really hard to come to a new country and start life from the beginning with new people, a new country, a new culture and a new language," she said Jalali said.
Today, Jalali has pivoted from medicine to technology. She is in her second year studying software engineering at Boise State University.
"I have my freedom here," she said. "For the first time, I feel that men and women are equal and everyone can build their life, their future and their career."
        "I'm happy to be here, but I can still say my soul is there."
Sabrina Sina, a Boise State political science graduate who arrived in the U.S. more than a decade ago, knows firsthand how difficult that adjustment can be.
"Being an English as a second language speaker is a struggle," Sina said.
Navigating higher education without an established support network meant balancing full-time work with classes. She credits campus resources for helping her push through.
"They do have advisors that help you more, and scholarships," Sina said. "Those really helped me, because being alone, not having support, working full time and going to school was part of making my dreams come true."
A community steps up
Across the Treasure Valley, neighbors and local organizations have stepped in to bridge the gap — offering everything from donated laptops and transportation aid to English classes.
Laura Armstrong is a co-founder of Glocal Community Partners, a Boise-based nonprofit that connects local volunteers with newly arrived refugees. She says their programs provide more than just practical skills.
"It's much more than just learning English," Armstrong said. "It's really a time for them to come together to socialize with one another."

title: Nampa City Council to consider water & irrigation system rate hikes
summary: The Nampa City Council is considering raising residential water rates. A public hearing has been scheduled for Monday, December 21 at Nampa City Hall.
text:
NAMPA, Idaho — The Nampa City Council is considering raising residential water rates.
A public hearing has been scheduled for Monday, December 21 at Nampa City Hall.
The City says rate hikes are needed for maintenance and the replacing of aging infrastructure.
If approved water customers would pay an average $1.48 more per month.
That amounts to an 8.4 percent increase, taking the average monthly water bill from $17.68 to $19.16.
But depending on what kind of service is used, some could see a spike of up to 13.8 percent. It all comes down to water gallon usage and lot size.
Nampa's water system includes more than 646 miles of pipe.
The City claims 112 miles of that is at or near the end of its lifespan, with 40 miles requiring immediate replacement.
Over the past year there were 63 domestic water and irrigation mainline breaks, which the City says can be more costly than the proposed upgrades.
As for irrigation services, that could go up by about $26.02 per year.
Those estimates are based on a 10,700-square-foot lot, with the current average bill for that size being $208.99 per year, or roughly $35 to $42 per month during the typical five- to six-month season.
—Nampa City Council to consider water & irrigation system rate hikes—
Nampa's irrigation system includes nearly 553 miles of pipe, with 95 miles at or near the end of its lifespan, and 18 miles in need of immediate replacement, per the City.
On top of all this, the City Council is looking to increase its revenue by implementing a 4.5 to 4.7 percent hike in water renewal rates.
That would add another $2.78 per month on average in bills.
Any changes would take effect March 1, 2027.
There are a couple of ways to offer your feedback.
First, you can attend the public hearing in person at Nampa City Hall.
Second, you may email comments to clerks@cityofnampa.us or mail them to the Clerk’s Office at 411 3rd St. S., Nampa, ID 83651.
Comments must be received by December 15, 2026.
The Clerk’s Office can be reached at (208) 468-5415 for additional options

title: A little-seen change in maternity billing codes could reveal a fuller picture of care
summary: For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way. Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of […]
text:
A little-seen change in maternity billing codes could reveal a fuller picture of care
Update won’t affect pregnant patients, but some obstetrics providers worry about how health insurers will adjust
A change to billing codes for pregnancy-related care beginning Jan. 1 will change the insurance process from one lump-sum payment billed at the end of a full pregnancy to separate services for the first time in 30 years. Providers say it won’t change much for patients, but will have many upsides for the overall provision of maternal care. (Photo by Noelle Straub/Stateline)
For decades, pregnancy has been approached by insurance companies as a singular event, with one payment at the end given to one provider, no matter how many prenatal visits occurred over the months or how straightforward or complex the pregnancy was along the way.
Beginning Jan. 1, that approach will change, with the unbundling of the codes providers use to bill insurance and receive payment for their services. The five-digit codes are used to describe the type of care a patient received, including specific procedures and testing.
While it isn’t expected to change much for patients, providers say it will make it easier to transfer care among clinics and hospitals, ease revenue burdens and perhaps most importantly, provide a more detailed and data-driven picture of maternity care nationwide that is opaque under the current system — though it remains somewhat unclear how private health insurance companies and Medicaid programs will respond to the change.
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, known as ACOG, worked with the American Medical Association to develop the new codes, which are then communicated to health insurers, including Medicaid. Pregnancies that began in the 2026 calendar year will likely still be billed under the global code, but those that have their first visit after Jan. 1 will use the new system.
Lisa Satterfield, vice president of practice, sustainability and workforce initiatives for ACOG, said the group started working on this change in 2022, after feedback from providers that the system was outdated.
“The way they were designed was for one provider to get billed from the very first prenatal visit to the very last postpartum visit,” Satterfield said. “It was not practical anymore.”
In the vast majority of cases, nothing should change about how much patients are paying for care, Satterfield said, because maternity visits are considered preventative care under the federal Affordable Care Act and not subject to cost sharing. Patients may just see more statements in the mail with an explanation of their benefits.
With the current global payment, no services are billed after the confirmation of a pregnancy until the last postpartum visit, Satterfield said, which leads to a long delay in the revenue from each visit in between. title: Meridian Speedway begins historic grandstand overhaul ahead of spring racing season
summary: 🏁 Meridian Speedway is getting a major upgrade! The historic 1964 North End grandstand is being replaced with new aluminum seating. What's your best memory at the track?
text:
MERIDIAN, Idaho — Changes are underway at Meridian Speedway, a racing venue that has been part of the community for generations, starting with its historic North End grandstand.
WATCH: Meridian Speedway replaces historic 1964 grandstand ahead of spring season
"The North End grandstand was originally built in 1964," said Adam Nelson, owner of the promotions group for the speedway, HWY 16.
More than 60 years later, those wooden bleachers are being replaced with a new aluminum grandstand. Part of the barn underneath is coming out, too.
"We are clearing the barn in between the maintenance shop and what we call the beer barn down at the end... and then... the midway is going to be double-width back now," said Colton Nelson, manager of HWY 16.
Colton Nelson said that will open up more room for food and drink stands, along with more space in the North End bleachers for people on busy race nights.
"It's generally the drinking section, the party section, the animals, and so they get a little rowdy and a little wild," Adam Nelson said.
When Idaho News 6 asked whether that was why the North End bleachers were the first to be replaced, Mike Murgoitio, a board member of Meridian Dairy Days & Stock Shows, laughed and said, "Yeah."
"They haven't been replaced, uh, since, you know, '64. They're due for an upgrade," Adam Nelson said.
RELATED | Revolution concert venue leaving Garden City after 14 years and opening new, larger home in Meridian
Even as the speedway changes, Colton Nelson, who grew up racing on the track, said keeping its history is part of the plan.
"My great grandpa raced here and promoted the Speedway. My grandpa raced here and promoted the Speedway. My father and uncles all raced here. And my dad's run the speedway here since '09, so I have, I have a rich bloodline with the Speedway here," Colton Nelson told me.
Johnny Giesler, another Meridian native, spent around 15 years racing at the speedway and even met his wife through racing.
RELATED | 'It was crazy': Neighbors react after Locust Grove overpass struck by a semi truck
"We grew up racing, and our parents were friends. Um, and then when I started driving for a race team that she drove for, then we started dating, um, and then we got married after that," Giesler said.
"We're investing in Meridian. We're built here, and we're still here, and we're going to continue that for legacies to come," Murgoitio said.
Work has already begun on the project, and the new, updated bleacher section is expected to be finished in time for the spring season.

title: Commentary: Lung cancer screening deserves attention for asbestos-exposed veterans in Idaho
summary: Without a doubt, the strength of the nation’s security is significantly rooted in the courage of citizens who endured the rigors of war zones and the vastness of the sea while fulfilling their commitment to fighting for liberty. In that spirit, the Navy’s birthday offers Idaho and the rest of the country a fitting opportunity […]
text:
Lung cancer screening deserves attention for asbestos-exposed veterans in Idaho
For Idaho veterans who may have endured serious contamination, advocacy should not disappear simply because it happened decades ago, writes guest columnist Cristina Johnson.
Naval Facilities Engineering Command Southwest public works employees inspect containment on a 2013 asbestos abatement project at Naval Base Coronado in California. (Photo by Mario T. Icari/U.S. Navy)
Without a doubt, the strength of the nation’s security is significantly rooted in the courage of citizens who endured the rigors of war zones and the vastness of the sea while fulfilling their commitment to fighting for liberty.
In that spirit, the Navy’s birthday offers Idaho and the rest of the country a fitting opportunity to honor those who answered the call to serve. Yet beyond tribute, this occasion is also an opportunity to remember that some of the profession’s consequences can last long after their retirement, especially for those previously stationed aboard older ships built with asbestos.
Valued for its heat and corrosion resistance, asbestos became widely used in military applications. It is now known to be a lung cancer risk decades after exposure, raising questions about whether they have adequate access to screening and information about their options.
    Idaho’s asbestos past reaches into military service
Idaho’s connection to military service is embodied in its roughly 121,300 veterans representing generations of Americans whose careers brought them into a range of branches, assignments and workplaces. For many of these retirees, however, their dedication may have also placed them in environments that heavily depended on asbestos.
Valued for its insulating and fireproofing properties, this natural mineral was extensively incorporated into countless structures and products the Navy relied on, especially in building ships prior to 1983, as well as in shipyards operating from the 1930s to the 1990s.
With this, it is not surprising that facilities such as the Naval Surface Warfare Center Detachment in Bayview contained asbestos materials. This pervasive presence has cost many lives before science revealed the toxicity of asbestos. Those exposed have become susceptible to lung cancer and other debilitating diseases even decades later.
Consistent with this, an interactive map indicates that just between 1999 and 2017, nearly 1,500 Idahoans have already succumbed to asbestos-associated illnesses, with 1,068 residents impacted by lung cancer and 267 and 161 more individuals lost to mesothelioma and asbestosis, respectively.
The reality is stark. The toll of this crisis is profound, and lung cancer accounts for the largest share of the deaths — surpassing both mesothelioma and asbestosis.

title: With no legal wins so far, Kalshi blocks operations in Utah
summary: Amid multiple legal disputes between Utah leaders and Kalshi, the prediction market platform has paused operations in the state. A spokesperson for Kalshi attributed the action “to the adverse final judgment in federal court,” in a lawsuit the company filed challenging a 2026 state law that included proposition bets in the definition of the state’s […]
text:
With no legal wins so far, Kalshi blocks operations in Utah
Company is immediately putting residency restrictions in place based on information users provided when opening their accounts
Kalshi photo illustration, Tuesday, April 7, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)
Amid multiple legal disputes between Utah leaders and Kalshi, the prediction market platform has paused operations in the state.
A spokesperson for Kalshi attributed the action “to the adverse final judgment in federal court,” in a lawsuit the company filed challenging a 2026 state law that included proposition bets in the definition of the state’s constitutional gambling ban, which allowed state officials to prohibit prediction market companies’ operations within state limits.
The company is immediately putting residency restrictions in place based on information users provided when opening their accounts, the spokesperson said, and then will enforce the block with a GPS-based tool.
As the company geofenced Utah, the court hasn’t yet ruled on a Commodity Futures Trading Commission emergency request for a relief “holding that Utah gambling laws are preempted and unenforceable,” since, the commission argues, derivatives markets are governed by federal law, according to the complaint.
“This is an unfortunate outcome for the more than 177,000 Utahns who use Kalshi. We will continue to fight this in court, and we look forward to returning to Utah once our legal position is vindicated,” Jacki McGavick, spokesperson for Kalshi said in a statement.
At the same time, Kalshi is also facing criminal charges in Utah — 12 online gambling promotion felony charges, one felony count of pattern of unlawful activity, and a misdemeanor charge for general gambling promotion according to charging documents filed by Utah Attorney General Derek Brown in October.
On Monday, Brown told reporters he was “thrilled” about Kalshi blocking operations in the state.
“We’ve asked them to follow the law. We’ve asked them that, ultimately, gambling products are illegal in Utah. It’s illegal under our state constitution, and we’re thrilled that they have made that decision,” Brown said. “And we’ll now look at what options we take at this point. But I’ll be meeting with my prosecutor shortly to figure out where we go at this point.”
While the state has secured a substantial legal victory in court, Kalshi has avoided criminal charges — similar to those filed in Utah — in Arizona courts.
Utah’s Attorney General also filed a civil lawsuit against Kalshi in October, accusing the company of a “brazen pattern of unlawful conduct.” Now that Kalshi has blocked its operations in the state, Brown said his office will review how that will affect that challenge.

title: National outages, emergency alerts become fodder for doomsday conspiracy theories
summary: Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days. Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst. The supposed warning signs? A nationwide […]
text:
National outages, emergency alerts become fodder for doomsday conspiracy theories
Online speculation comes as country’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats
Cases of bottled water are displayed for sale at a Costco in Burbank, Calif. Doomsday conspiracy theories circulating online have fueled calls for Americans to stockpile food, water and emergency supplies amid unfounded predictions of widespread blackouts and other catastrophes. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Stock up on food and medicine. Fill containers with water. Prepare to live off the grid for at least 90 days.
Those were among the warnings circulating on social media in recent weeks, as online posts predicted a looming national catastrophe and urged Americans to prepare for the worst.
The supposed warning signs? A nationwide flight shutdown, disruptions to banking and technology services and a routine federal emergency alert test — seemingly unrelated events that some online users portrayed as evidence of a coordinated cyberattack or impending emergency.
The doomsday predictions lack credible evidence. But the speculation comes as the nation’s aging infrastructure faces mounting vulnerabilities from extreme weather, rising energy demands and cyberthreats — raising legitimate questions about the country’s preparedness for major disruptions.
Federal officials have said they found no evidence that the latest disruptions were connected or that a nationwide emergency was imminent. And some emergency management experts warn that false alarms can undermine public trust in official warnings and complicate disaster response when real emergencies strike.
Still, the attention surrounding these unfounded predictions does not necessarily mean they have gained widespread acceptance.
Joseph Uscinski, a political science professor at the University of Miami who studies conspiracy theories, cautioned against interpreting viral posts as evidence of a broader shift in public beliefs.
“Your average conspiracy theory dies on the vine,” he said, noting that many fade as the news cycle moves on.
Uscinski described the reaction as a recurring pattern: A major event sparks conspiracy theories, those claims attract attention and then eventually fade, only for the cycle to repeat when another event captures the public’s attention.
Some of the latest rumors appeared to gain traction ahead of Tuesday’s nationwide Emergency Alert System test, which interrupted television and radio broadcasts across the country. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA, and the Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, had announced the Nov. 17 test in September as part of routine efforts to evaluate the nation’s emergency warning infrastructure. Federal rules require nationwide testing at least once every three years.

title: Commentary: Idahoans should know about the brazen new plan to sell our public lands
summary: This election season, public lands were on the ballot. The issue showed up in campaigns across the country, including here in Idaho where we reelected leaders who have made this position clear: Public lands are not for sale. One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions […]
text:
Idahoans should know about the brazen new plan to sell our public lands
The US Department of Interior just released a strategic plan that, for the first time ever, prioritizes selling public land under its control, writes guest columnist Rob Mason.
The Lewis Clark National Historic Trail, as seen near the Lemhi Pass in Idaho. Today the pass is traversed by a 35-mile long graded unpaved Backcountry Byway through public lands where colorful wildflowers like arrowleaf balsam-root, lupine and delphinium rival the sunset. (Photo by Bob Wick/Bureau of Land Management)
This election season, public lands were on the ballot. The issue showed up in campaigns across the country, including here in Idaho where we reelected leaders who have made this position clear: Public lands are not for sale.
One recent poll showed 96% of Idahoans oppose selling public land, so it turns out these positions are also smart politics. It’s not everyday that you see an issue with such broad bipartisan support all across the state.
New poll finds 96% Idaho voters say public lands should remain in public hands
We’re fortunate to have U.S. Congressman Mike Simpson and U.S. Sens. Jim Risch and Mike Crapo on our side as advocates for keeping public lands in public hands, because unfortunately the attacks on our outdoor heritage just don’t seem to be going away.
The latest example sadly comes directly from the U.S. Department of Interior, which just released a strategic plan that, for the first time ever, prioritizes selling public land under its control. Here in Idaho, that most likely means they could be selling off our treasured Bureau of Land Management lands.
Interior’s plan says the agency will “work to decrease the size of the federal estate.” In other words, it plans to sell our public lands. Its approach is not a narrow, targeted one meant to solve a specific local problem, where transferring a small piece of public land to a local government might make sense from time to time.
Instead, this Department of the Interior appears intent on trying to sell off as much of our public land as it can. There’s no acreage limit, no ceiling on how much public land could be sold, and no endpoint for the sell-off.
The plan calls for public lands to be sold to state and local governments, but those governments are unlikely to be able to afford the long-term costs of land management and will be forced to find a way to make a profit from the land. Ultimately that means many of those formerly-public lands will be privatized, commercialized, or both. Think data center developers aren’t paying attention to this?
At a time when Americans are rightly up in arms about the rapid, irresponsible construction of data centers, it’s hard to understand why the administration would pursue a policy that could allow them to be built even faster by selling BLM lands that may ultimately end up in the hands of data center developers.
